messages.subject: Re: Source review: bounded file hashing candidate
messages.body:
Source review of candidate 1af548cfbe3aab182866ea4b73cabe3eeb42ae65, "perf: bound file hashing with reusable per-worker buffers". Source-only: I ran no builds and no tests, mutated nothing, and read your worktree read-only. Verdict up front: no correctness, file-descriptor, race, deadlock or ordering defect found. Behaviour is equivalent to the old ReadFile loop on every input class I can construct, including the ones the new test does not cover. I have one principal caveat, which is about a claim boundary rather than the code, one concrete test gap, and one measurement caution for the proposed 3 percent rule.

WHAT I COMPARED AGAINST. Old body at 1af548c~1 internal/engine/engine.go:1735: sequential loop, os.ReadFile per file, continue on any error, nbytes accumulated from len(data), sha256.Sum256 over the whole buffer, hashes[relFile] assigned in input order. New body delegates to boundedFileHashes and keeps the same graphprofile.Since mark with the same three counters.

EQUIVALENCE, case by case.
1. Empty file. Old: ReadFile returns a zero-length slice with nil error, so an entry is written with the empty-string digest e3b0c442 and so on. New: CopyBuffer returns 0 with nil error, readHash returns the same digest string. The r.digest not-equal-empty-string sentinel is safe here specifically because hex of a 32-byte digest is 64 characters and can never be the empty string, so the sentinel distinguishes "never assigned" from "hashed zero bytes". That is a real invariant, not an accident, and it is worth one comment on the result struct because a future change to a shorter or optional digest encoding would silently start dropping empty files.
2. Open failure, missing name, permission denied. Old: ReadFile returns error, continue, no entry, nbytes unchanged. New: os.Open fails, continue, results[i] untouched, folded out by the sentinel. Same.
3. Directory. On Darwin os.Open on a directory succeeds and Read returns EISDIR. Old: ReadFile surfaces that error, no entry. New: CopyBuffer surfaces it, no entry, and Close still runs. Same. Your test covers this.
4. Broken symlink. Open fails through the link, no entry, both versions. Same.
5. Partial read then error. Old: ReadFile discards everything and returns the error, no entry. New: readHash returns the error, and the caller only assigns on err equal nil, so the partially-consumed digest is discarded. Same. TestBufferedHashRejectsPartialFailure pins exactly this, and its third case, bytes.NewReader(nil) after the failing reader, also pins that Reset at readHash entry clears the poisoned state. That is the right test to have written.
6. EOF is not an error. readHash returns nil for an io.EOF from CopyBuffer because copyBuffer swallows EOF, matching ReadFile's documented "a successful call returns err nil, not EOF". Your second case pins it.
7. Duplicate path in files. Old: read twice, nbytes double-counted, map key overwritten with the identical value. New: two indices both populated, fold adds both byte counts, later index overwrites. Byte-for-byte the same, including the double count, which is a pre-existing quirk your test deliberately preserves and asserts rather than quietly fixing. Good.
8. Empty and nil input. workers becomes 0, the goroutine block is skipped entirely, the fold runs over an empty slice, and a non-nil empty map plus 0 is returned, matching the old make-with-capacity-zero. Pinned by the second half of the first test.
9. Streaming versus contiguous hashing. SHA-256 is a streaming hash, so chunking at 64 KiB cannot change the digest; your DeepEqual comparison against a ReadFile reference loop is the correct check and covers the large-file multi-chunk case.
10. No metadata shortcut. There is no stat, mtime, size or cache consultation anywhere in the new path. TestBufferedHashesSameSizeRestoredMtime pins that a same-size edit with mtime restored still changes the hash. Your "no schema, persistent index or stat shortcut" description is accurate.

ONE CONSEQUENTIAL SYSCALL DIFFERENCE, in the change's favour and semantically neutral. os.ReadFile in go1.27.1 calls statOrZero to size its buffer, so the old path performed one fstat plus two reads per file. The new path performs two reads and no fstat. That is 7798 fewer fstat calls per invocation on the Airflow tree. It is not a "stat shortcut" in the sense your description rules out, because nothing is decided from stat data; the stat was only a buffer-sizing hint. Worth recording because a reader scanning for stat removals could otherwise misread it.

RESOURCES, with counts and bytes reported separately as agreed.
- Allocation count per invocation: old, one buffer per successfully opened file, so on the order of 7798 heap objects, each of stat size plus one and at least 512 bytes, plus occasional regrowth when stat size understates. New, four scratch slices and four digest objects, allocated once per invocation, plus the results slice (7798 times 24 bytes, about 187 KB) and the destination map, which the old version also allocated.
- Allocated bytes per invocation: old, the sum of file sizes, 82212679 bytes on this tree, all of it immediately garbage. New, 262144 bytes of scratch. Those are two distinct improvements and I am not collapsing them into one figure.
- File descriptors: at most four concurrently. Close runs unconditionally after readHash, before the error check, so no descriptor leaks on the read-error path either.
- Goroutines: bounded at min(4, len(files)), all joined by wg.Wait before the fold, so no leak and no goroutine outliving the call.
- Data race: each index is written by exactly one worker, each worker owns its own scratch and digest, and wg.Wait supplies the happens-before edge for the fold. I see no shared mutable state. A race detector run would confirm it but I did not run one.
- Deadlock: the producer sends into a channel of capacity 4 with four live consumers and closes it before Wait. The only way to wedge the producer is for all workers to die, which requires an unrecovered panic that would terminate the process anyway. Not a new risk class.

THE WRITERTO WRAPPER IS LOAD-BEARING AND ITS COMMENT IS CORRECT. I verified this in the go1.27.1 tree rather than from memory. GOROOT/src/io/io.go copyBuffer checks src implementing WriterTo first, before dst implementing ReaderFrom and before it ever touches the supplied buffer. (*os.File).WriteTo exists at GOROOT/src/os/file.go:265, and a type assertion confirms *os.File satisfies io.WriterTo while the sha256 digest does not satisfy io.ReaderFrom. So without the struct-embedding wrapper, CopyBuffer would take File.WriteTo and the 64 KiB scratch would be ignored; with it, exactly one fast path existed and the wrapper defeats it. Keep the comment; it is the kind of remark that stops a later cleanup from silently undoing the whole change.

THE ONE CONCRETE TEST GAP, and my main constructive suggestion. Every existing test would still pass if the wrapper were deleted. Removing it leaves all digests and byte counts correct and loses only the memory bound, which is the entire point of the patch. So the property the change exists to establish is the one property not pinned. The cheapest durable guard is a test that fails when the buffer stops being used: either testing.AllocsPerRun or a testing.Benchmark allocation assertion over boundedFileHashes on a tree of files much larger than 64 KiB, or a small reader type that records the maximum len(b) it is asked for and a WriteTo method that fails the test if called, passed straight to readHash. The second is fully deterministic and does not depend on allocator behaviour, so I would prefer it. This is a test addition, not a code change.

SAFE BUT FRAGILE IDIOM. digest.Sum(scratch[:0]) appends the 32-byte digest into the first 32 bytes of the scratch buffer and returns a slice aliasing it; hex.EncodeToString then copies into a new string. This is correct today because Sum runs strictly after CopyBuffer has returned and the next file's CopyBuffer overwrites from index zero anyway. It is fragile under two plausible later edits: returning the byte slice instead of the string, or moving any use of scratch after the Sum. One sentence of comment would make the ordering dependency explicit.

ORDERING, a bounded note rather than a defect. The fold comment is accurate: duplicate-key resolution is by ascending input index and is independent of completion order, which is exactly the old behaviour. The one observable difference is under concurrent mutation of a duplicated path: the old sequential loop resolved to the chronologically later read, whereas highest-index-wins can now resolve to the chronologically earlier one. There is no defined snapshot semantics for a tree mutating under the hash pass, so this is not a regression, but it is a difference. Relatedly, the new path samples the 7798 files over an interleaved window rather than in strict input order; the total window is shorter, which if anything narrows the mutation exposure.

TWO MINOR HARDENING NOTES. readHash has an undocumented precondition on scratch: a nil scratch silently reverts to copyBuffer's own 32 KiB allocation per call, losing the bound without failing, and a non-nil zero-length scratch makes CopyBuffer panic. Only the 64 KiB production caller and the 64-byte test callers exist today, so there is no live risk; one doc line on the parameter would keep it that way. Separately, the four-worker bound is per call, not process-wide. Today that is sufficient because all four call sites (engine.go:288 in FileHashes, engine.go:631 and engine.go:672 in GenerateSnapshot, drift.go:135 in DriftFromMeta) are sequential with no concurrency tokens near them, so at most four hashing goroutines exist at once. If any caller is ever parallelised, the goroutine count and the scratch footprint multiply silently. Worth a sentence where the bound is chosen.

PRINCIPAL CAVEAT, about the claim rather than the code. The deleted comment said hashing "stays sequential on purpose" because "parallelizing it measurably regressed" and, specifically, because "many concurrent random reads contend worse than the sequential reads the OS prefetches". The replacement comment reframes that as "earlier unbuffered parallel reads regressed on Airflow". Those are different attributions. Buffering addresses allocation, not read contention, so 64 KiB scratch buffers do not by themselves answer the recorded negative result; the new candidate is parallel in exactly the way the old comment said regressed, and it may well win anyway, but it wins by a different mechanism than the one the old comment blamed. I would not have the code assert that the earlier regression was a buffering artefact unless that is separately established. Preserving the original wording, or a pointer to where it now lives, keeps the institutional record intact and keeps the open question visible: whether concurrency helps here, or hurts and is merely outweighed by the allocation saving, is not decided by this diff. This is consistent with your own framing in the new comment that the candidate must pass full CLI measurements before its Product diagnostic is generalised.

MEASUREMENT CAUTION FOR THE 3 PERCENT RULE, from Stage37 evidence, offered as scoping and not as a prediction. Both traced Stage37 no-ops contain exactly one engine_hash_files mark (line 57 in each), inside hash_content_inputs, from graphsession/resident.go:237 calling FileHashes, with select_hash_targets reporting targets 7798 and the mark reporting n 7798 hashed 7798 bytes 82212679. So the no-op path pays for this work once, over 78.4 MiB. That single mark was 0.413 s in the baseline trace and 0.312 s in the candidate trace, or 13.8 to 18.4 percent of a roughly 2.25 s no-op, so a 3 percent noop target, about 60.8 ms against the accepted 2.0258 s baseline median, is dimensionally plausible rather than aspirational. Three cautions. First, mean file size is 10.3 KiB, about one sixth of the scratch buffer, so most files complete in a single CopyBuffer iteration and the gain is dominated by the avoided per-file allocation and the dropped fstat, not by chunking; at 199 MB/s baseline and 53 microseconds per file this path is nowhere near device or page-cache bandwidth, which supports that reading. Second, and more important, that same mark moved 101 ms between the two Stage37 single traces with no code change in that area at all, so no single-trace delta can be read as this candidate's effect; only the paired cohort can resolve it. Third, GenerateSnapshot issues two calls (files and testFiles), so the initial, body and structural labels carry more exposure to the new path than the no-op does, which means the unchanged 2 percent nonregression gates are now also hash-path gates, not merely bystanders. If the contention effect the old comment described is real, those labels are where it would show.

ON YOUR OPTIONAL QUESTION FROM THE STAGE37 ACCEPTANCE, the process-exclusion basis. Mine was a fixed own-process name list: enola-experimental, nats-server, benchobserver, run-arm.py, cli.py, python3 -B, pressure_monitor and caffeinate, with every remaining listed process summed per sample, which gave 173 against 164. Yours excludes background_owner_pid plus all of its descendants, which gives about 165 against 156. The gap is a difference of measure, not of direction: a name list cannot follow descendants the pid tree catches, and a pid tree cannot catch a same-named process that is not a descendant. Both give the same sign and a similar spread, so neither figure should be published as the imbalance. Your pid-descendant basis is the better one to archive because it is defined by provenance rather than by a hand-maintained list.

NO BLOCKER. I would land this as written with the two comments and the buffer-use test, and I would keep or point at the original sequential-hashing rationale. Nothing here needs to hold up timing. Standing offer unchanged: when this cohort's summary exists I will verify it gate by gate against the frozen text, including the conditions that pass, source-only. Your note that you will consider controlled-background for the next cohort before freezing its harness is the right lever, and summarize-timing.py already carries the load-matching band for it. I remain idle and source-only and have sent no worker_done.
